Pregnancy and Lactation Drug Reference

Therapeutic classes and drug names in alphabetical order.

Overview

About this reference

This offline compilation reproduces the supplied drug assessments for study. Clinical accuracy and the cited publications were not independently verified.

Source records remain separate where a drug occurs more than once. Grouped products remain together. Open a row’s source label to see its original section and references.

The eight DOCX files cover entries 1–395 in 387 rows. Four rows contain grouped entries. The original OpenEvidence HTML supplies 212 additional source rows.

DOCX 01-17
DOCX 01-17 · 01. ACE Inhibitors & Angiotensin Receptor Blockers · source entry 1Open source details
❌ AVOID / UNSAFE
❌ CONTRAINDICATED
✅ SAFE
✅ SAFE
Fetotoxic, especially in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters: renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, lung hypoplasia, IUGR, fetal death. Stop as soon as pregnancy is detected. Captopril is one of the preferred antihypertensives during breastfeeding because milk levels are very low (ESC 2025; AHA/ACC). Use caution in preterm neonates.

⚠️ CAUTION (single exposure acceptable)
Causes dose-dependent uterine relaxation , which raises PPH risk at delivery. Halothane hepatitis risk. Animal developmental toxicity data exist. Sevoflurane or isoflurane are preferred. First-line analgesic in pregnancy (ACOG). Keep paracetamol at or below 4 g/day and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time. Compatible with breastfeeding; with high caffeine intake, watch for infant irritability or poor sleep.

The label warns of embryo-fetal toxicity: neural tube defects in hamsters at 2.6× the maximum daily dose. NOWS risk. Drug / productPregnancyLactationKey notes
Albendazole
OpenEvidence · 03 · Refs: [4], [13], [14], [15]
OpenEvidence · 03 · 03. Antiviral & antiparasitic agents · Antiviral & antiparasitic agents · table row 5Open source details
❌ AVOID / UNSAFE
Avoid, especially in the first trimester. Embryotoxic with skeletal malformations in rats and rabbits at doses below human doses. Single-dose human exposure is reassuring, but this can't be extrapolated to multiple-dose courses. Label: pregnancy test before treatment; effective contraception during treatment and for 1 month after. WHO allows single-dose deworming in the second and third trimesters in endemic areas
A single dose is acceptable (WHO); minimal excretion into milk. Long courses (e.g., echinococcosis): no data

SAFE
Converted to methimazole. Methimazole embryopathy: aplasia cutis, choanal/esophageal atresia, abdominal wall defects, VSD. Korean cohort: +17.1 malformations per 1,000 live births vs +8.8 with PTU. ATA 2026: PTU preferred in the 1st trimester if available; switching from methimazole to PTU in the 1st trimester did not lower malformation risk. Whether to switch back after 16 weeks is unsettled. Oral Antidiabetics — source notes

Insulin is preferred in pregnancy. Switch oral agents to insulin before conception or when pregnancy is confirmed. Metformin (and rarely glibenclamide) is an acceptable alternative when insulin is declined or not feasible.

Metformin component (#45, 47, 49, 53). Pregnancy: acceptable alternative to insulin. It crosses the placenta freely, data on offspring adiposity are inconsistent, and the treatment-failure rate is high. Lactation: compatible; infant dose is about 0.11–1% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose and no adverse infant effects have been reported.

Antidotes & Antagonists — source notes

In life-threatening poisoning, maternal resuscitation comes first. Do not withhold an indicated antidote because the patient is pregnant.

Antimalarials — source notes

Untreated malaria in pregnancy causes miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and maternal death. Treat promptly.

Antineoplastics — source notes

General rules

Pregnancy:

Avoid all cytotoxic chemotherapy in T1.

Agents marked "T2/T3" may be given after organogenesis.

Stop chemotherapy after 35 weeks so marrow can recover before delivery.

Use a multidisciplinary oncology–MFM team.

Lactation: breastfeeding is not recommended during active chemotherapy, endocrine or targeted therapy.

Pregnancy & Lactation Safety Reference — Drugs 100–155 (Classes 24–31)

pregnancy-lactation-safety-drugs-100-155.docx

Legend

SAFE: acceptable or preferred; adequate human data or extensive experience

CAUTION: use only if benefit outweighs risk, or only with the conditions stated (trimester, dose, duration, monitoring)

AVOID: insufficient data or a signal of harm; use a safer alternative

CONTRAINDICATED: known or strongly suspected fetal or infant harm

Ratings assume usual therapeutic doses in an otherwise healthy patient. A life-threatening maternal condition can justify a drug rated CAUTION or AVOID.

Contraindicated / clearly avoid (summary): apixaban, rivaroxaban (pregnancy), cilostazol, miltefosine, tinidazole (1st trimester), molnupiravir, nintedanib, alendronate/ibandronate (± cholecalciferol), and the oral pseudoephedrine combination (1st trimester and lactation).

Safe-choice alternatives: LMWH or UFH for anticoagulation; metronidazole (standard-dose regimens, not single high doses) for nitroimidazole-responsive infections; labetalol or propranolol for beta-blockade; nirmatrelvir-ritonavir or remdesivir for COVID-19; inhaled budesonide, salbutamol or ipratropium for asthma; saline or an intranasal corticosteroid for congestion.

Pregnancy & Lactation Safety Reference: Drugs 156–199 (Classes 32–42)

pregnancy-lactation-safety-drugs-156-199.docx

Legend

SAFE: acceptable or preferred; adequate human data or extensive experience

CAUTION: use only if benefit outweighs risk, or only with the conditions stated (trimester, dose, duration, monitoring)

AVOID: insufficient data or a signal of harm; use a safer alternative

CONTRAINDICATED: known or strongly suspected fetal or infant harm

Ratings assume usual therapeutic doses in an otherwise healthy patient. A life-threatening maternal condition can justify a drug rated CAUTION or AVOID. For psychiatric and seizure disorders, stopping an effective drug carries its own risk of relapse; do not stop abruptly without specialist input.

Contraindicated / clearly avoid (summary): amiodarone (outside emergencies), amlodipine + atenolol (switch combination), primidone, flunarizine, pramipexole/ropinirole (lactation), tetrabenazine, clozapine (lactation), alprazolam, chlordiazepoxide, vinpocetine, and the cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

Safe-choice alternatives: nifedipine, amlodipine alone or labetalol for blood pressure; adenosine, then beta-blockers or verapamil for SVT; lamotrigine or levetiracetam for epilepsy; sertraline for depression; sumatriptan for acute migraine and propranolol for prevention; quetiapine or olanzapine (or the antipsychotic that already works) for psychosis or bipolar disorder; lorazepam if a benzodiazepine is unavoidable; prednisolone as the systemic glucocorticoid.

Ratings assume usual therapeutic doses in an otherwise healthy patient. A life-threatening maternal condition can justify a drug rated CAUTION or AVOID. For immunosuppressants, stopping an effective drug risks disease flare or graft rejection, which itself harms pregnancy outcomes; do not stop without specialist input.

Insulins — source notes

All insulins are SAFE during breastfeeding (insulin is a protein that is digested in the infant gut) and are preferred over newer non-insulin diabetes drugs postpartum. Insulin requirements fall sharply after delivery; reduce doses to avoid hypoglycemia.

Ratings assume usual therapeutic doses in an otherwise healthy patient. A life-threatening maternal condition can justify a drug rated CAUTION or AVOID. Pregnancy & Lactation Safety Chart – Part 4 (Drugs 200–249)

pregnancy-lactation-safety-200-249.docx

Grading key

SAFE – Compatible; adequate human data or negligible systemic absorption.

CAUTION – Use only if clearly needed, or only under the stated restriction (trimester, dose, area, infant age).

AVOID – Risk or lack of data outweighs benefit; use an alternative.

CONTRAINDICATED – Known or strongly suspected harm.

Grades assume standard doses and routes. Topical grades assume limited body-surface area and avoidance of application to the breast/nipple during breastfeeding.

Summary – clearly unsafe in pregnancy: Acitretin, Finasteride, Spironolactone (and Furosemide + Spironolactone), Fluocinolone + Hydroquinone + Tretinoin, Triamterene + HCTZ, Bismuth subsalicylate, Eplerenone, Hydroxyethyl starch, IV Fructose, Betahistine.

Summary – avoid during breastfeeding: Acitretin, Finasteride, Fluocinolone + Hydroquinone + Tretinoin, Oxybenzone/Octinoxate/Enzacamene-containing sunscreens, Triamterene + HCTZ, Bismuth subsalicylate, Cinnarizine + Dimenhydrinate.

Preferred substitutes: Mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen; calcium/aluminium/magnesium antacids before PPIs; loperamide for diarrhoea; doxylamine–pyridoxine or meclizine for nausea; spironolactone (not eplerenone) for postpartum MRA need; hydrochlorothiazide alone rather than triamterene combination postpartum.

This chart is a reference aid; individual decisions should weigh indication, gestational age, dose, duration and infant age/prematurity.

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety for this group depends on a few class-specific concerns: aminoglycoside ototoxicity in the fetus, tetracycline effects on teeth and bone, fluoroquinolone cartilage concerns, macrolide signals (especially clarithromycin), chloramphenicol "gray baby" syndrome, and the fact that first-line TB therapy is continued in pregnancy.

Most β-lactams are first-line in both pregnancy and breastfeeding: penicillins, cephalosporins, and meropenem. Vancomycin, clindamycin, metronidazole, erythromycin, azithromycin, and first-line TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) are also acceptable.[1][2][3][4]

Avoid or reserve these in pregnancy:

  • Tetracyclines after the first trimester. They discolor teeth and inhibit bone growth.
  • Streptomycin and amikacin. Both can cause irreversible fetal deafness; with streptomycin the risk is about 10%.
  • Clarithromycin.
  • Chloramphenicol near term. It can cause gray baby syndrome.
  • Rifaximin in the first trimester.
  • Fluoroquinolones, unless no safer alternative exists.
  • Amoxicillin–clavulanate in women at risk of preterm delivery. In ORACLE I it raised proven necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) from 0.5% to 1.9%.[5][6][7][2][8][9][10]

During breastfeeding, nearly every agent here is compatible. The main exceptions:

  • Chloramphenicol: avoid.
  • Doxycycline: limit to short courses of up to about 21 days.
  • Macrolides in the first 2 postpartum weeks: linked to infantile pyloric stenosis.
  • Clindamycin, metronidazole, and fluoroquinolones: watch the infant for diarrhea or thrush.[4][11][12][13]

Penicillins and β-lactamase inhibitor combinations

In the Cochrane review of antibiotics for preterm rupture of membranes, the NEC signal is confined to the β-lactam subgroup that includes co-amoxiclav, and ORACLE I drives it.[19]

Figure 1.5 Comparison 1 Any antibiotic versus placebo, Outcome 5 Neonatal necrotising enterocolitis.

Cephalosporins and carbapenem

Macrolides

Across all macrolides, first-trimester exposure carried an aRR of 1.55 for major malformations and 1.62 for cardiovascular malformations compared with penicillin in a UK cohort of 104,605 children. Miscarriage risk was higher in observational studies (pooled OR 1.82).[24][26]

Other antibacterials

Antitubercular agents

Where sources disagree

  • Macrolides and pyloric stenosis:
    • In a Danish cohort of about 1 million births, maternal macrolide use in postpartum days 0–13 gave an RR of 3.49 (absolute increase 2.15 per 1,000), with a possible link in late pregnancy.
    • A meta-analysis found no significant association with breastfeeding (OR 0.96) or with pregnancy exposure (OR 1.15).[11][49]
  • Azithromycin and erythromycin in early pregnancy:
    • The US HIV OI guideline prefers azithromycin, and one review lists erythromycin as the only recommended macrolide.
    • The UK MHRA judged the evidence too weak to exclude a small increase in malformation risk with azithromycin or clarithromycin.[2][24][50][22]
  • Fluoroquinolones, doxycycline, and metronidazole in lactation:
    • Current US labels advise against breastfeeding or recommend pump-and-discard: for 2 days with ciprofloxacin, and for 48 h with metronidazole.
    • LactMed and AFP consider short courses acceptable.
    • For metronidazole, the label notes that infant serum levels can approach therapeutic levels. Another review estimates that 0.9% of the maternal dose reaches the infant.[16][5][4][51][33][34]
  • Pyridoxine for breastfed infants: the ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline cites the AAP in recommending pyridoxine for exclusively breastfed infants of mothers on isoniazid. The current AAP Red Book recommends it only if the infant is receiving isoniazid.[1][7]
  • Co-amoxiclav and NEC: later lower-quality studies did not reproduce the ORACLE signal, but guidelines still advise avoiding it in preterm delivery.[18]

Practical points

  • Rifampicin interactions: rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer. It makes hormonal contraception unreliable postpartum (use an IUD or barrier method) and lowers levels of nifedipine, other CCBs, and many other drugs on earlier lists. Levothyroxine requirements may rise. All of this is standard practice.
  • Gentamicin monitoring: check levels and renal function. Avoid combining it with furosemide or vancomycin when possible, because ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity add up.[6]
  • Chlamydia in pregnancy: use azithromycin in place of doxycycline (standard practice).[2]
  • Inadvertent early exposure to doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone in the first trimester has not been linked to higher malformation rates. Counsel the patient, but this alone does not justify termination.[33][5]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety here depends on route (topical/vaginal vs systemic), dose, and trimester, especially for azoles like fluconazole, where high-dose first-trimester exposure carries a different risk than a single low dose.

Still open: lactation data for each agent, and the pregnancy data for miconazole oral gel, luliconazole, and the newer large cohort studies.

Still open: lactation data for voriconazole, nystatin, ciclopirox, and topical ketoconazole/miconazole, and how much oral miconazole gel is absorbed systemically.

Topical azoles (miconazole), nystatin, and topical ciclopirox are the safest options in both pregnancy and lactation. Voriconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole (especially high-dose or in the first trimester) should be avoided in pregnancy. Fluconazole is one of the preferred systemic antifungals during breastfeeding.[1][2][3][4]

Topical agents are generally considered safe in pregnancy because very little reaches the bloodstream.[5][6] For serious invasive fungal infections in pregnancy, amphotericin B is the treatment of choice, not an azole.[1]

Summary by agent

Fluconazole: risk by dose

  • High dose (≥400 mg/day through the first trimester): linked to a recognized pattern of birth defects, including brachycephaly, cleft palate, femoral bowing, arthrogryposis, and congenital heart disease.[11][9]
  • Low dose (single 150 mg): evidence is conflicting.
    • A US Medicaid cohort found a small increase in musculoskeletal malformations (aRR 1.30), about 12 extra cases per 10,000 exposed pregnancies.[21]
    • A 2024 meta-analysis found no increase in overall major malformations after adjustment (ORa 1.02), but did find a higher miscarriage risk (ORa 1.60).[22]
  • HIV opportunistic infection guidelines advise against fluconazole at any dose for vulvovaginal candidiasis in the first trimester. After the first trimester, fluconazole or itraconazole may be considered for serious infections.[9]

The Danish nationwide cohort (NEJM) below shows fluconazole outcomes by cumulative dose. Overall birth defects were not increased, but tetralogy of Fallot stood out:

Figure 2 Association of First-Trimester Exposure to Oral Fluconazole with the Risk of Birth Defects Overall and 15 Specific Birth Defects. In the analysis of birth defects overall, infants with more than one anomaly were counted only once. In the analysis of specific birth defects, affected infants were assigned to as many of the birth-defect categories as their International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, codes in the first year of life indicated. Prevalence odds ratios were adjusted for calendar year; maternal parity; age at pregnancy onset; place of birth; place of residence in Denmark; level of education; marital status; family income; and status with respect to smoking during pregnancy, previous births with congenital malformations, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, other sexually transmitted diseases, other infectious diseases, other immunodeficient states, receipt of clinical care for high-risk pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, and treatment with immunosuppressive agents, oral antibiotics, oral corticosteroids, antiepileptic agents, oral contraceptives, or drugs for in vitro fertilization. However, in the analyses of specific birth defects, HIV infection, other sexually transmitted diseases, and other immunodeficient states were diagnosed in only a few mothers, and only a few mothers filled prescriptions for oral corticosteroids or antiepileptic agents; these covariates therefore could not be included in the adjusted analyses. The number of unexposed pregnancies included in the analyses was 968,236. NE denotes not estimable.

Practical points

  • Product names: this table assumes Fungidal and Clopirox are skin or vaginal products. Oral or systemic forms of ketoconazole, miconazole, or terbinafine change the risk. Oral ketoconazole should be avoided during breastfeeding because of liver toxicity.[15]
  • Miconazole oral gel and warfarin: the oral gel substantially raises INR in patients on warfarin (mean rise 1.27; 30% had INR >5). Use nystatin instead.[24][25]
  • Applying to the breast: use water-miscible creams or gels rather than ointments, which expose the infant to mineral paraffins.[15][20][4]
  • Onychomycosis and other non-urgent conditions: reasonable to postpone systemic treatment until after pregnancy.[17]

Safety turns on systemic vs topical exposure and trimester, particularly for the benzimidazoles and ivermectin, and on ganciclovir's known teratogenicity in animals. I'll check the pregnancy registry data and the lactation data for each agent.

Still open: lactation data for the anthelmintics and permethrin, crotamiton safety in pregnancy, mebendazole cohort data, and how much acyclovir and valacyclovir pass into breast milk.

Acyclovir, valacyclovir, permethrin 5%, and docosanol are the safe choices in both pregnancy and lactation. Ganciclovir should be avoided in both. Albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin fall in between: animal data raise concern, but human data are reassuring. Their use is generally kept to the second or third trimester, or to cases where no alternative fits.[1][2][3][4][5]

Summary by agent

Where sources disagree

  • Permethrin in lactation: the older US label suggests pausing breastfeeding, based on tumors in animals. LactMed and BASHH consider it acceptable because so little is absorbed.[2][24][21]
  • Ivermectin: the CDC classes it as low risk and probably compatible with breastfeeding. BASHH and a Lancet review on soil-transmitted helminths do not recommend it in pregnancy or lactation. 2026 data from the BOHEMIA trials on inadvertent early-pregnancy exposure had confidence intervals too wide to rule out harm or benefit.[7][2][17][14]
  • Mebendazole: in a small 2026 German Embryotox cohort, 6.67% of 75 infants had major malformations (3 heart defects). The confidence interval was wide, the authors drew no conclusion about teratogenic risk, and larger studies show no signal.[13]

Practical points

  • Higher acyclovir dose in pregnancy: faster kidney clearance in pregnancy means suppressive acyclovir is given as 400 mg three times daily, more than in non-pregnant patients. ACOG recommends offering suppressive therapy from 36 weeks to women with a history of genital herpes.[1][3]
  • Severe or disseminated HSV in pregnancy: give IV acyclovir. HSV hepatitis is rare but can be fatal.[1][3]
  • Untreated helminths also carry risk: untreated soil-transmitted helminth infection in pregnancy is linked to maternal iron-deficiency anemia, low birth weight, and maternal and neonatal death. Weigh this when deciding whether to delay treatment.[16]
  • If albendazole is started and pregnancy occurs: the label says to stop it immediately.[4]
  • Topicals near the breast: use water-miscible creams or gels rather than ointments, so the infant doesn't ingest mineral paraffins.[21][8]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety here depends on RAAS blockade, which is fetotoxic in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, on atenolol's link to fetal growth restriction, on statins now being permitted in high-risk pregnancy, and on low-dose aspirin being used for preeclampsia prophylaxis while clopidogrel data remain sparse.

Still open: the updated statin guidance, trimetazidine, prazosin, the thiazides and indapamide in lactation, and amlodipine and atenolol in breastfeeding.

Still open: trimetazidine and indapamide specifically, and aspirin and clopidogrel in breastfeeding.

Safe or preferred in both pregnancy and breastfeeding: nifedipine, metoprolol, digoxin, and low-dose aspirin (under 100 mg). Amlodipine, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, prazosin, and nitroglycerin are acceptable when clearly needed. Nifedipine is a first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy alongside labetalol, which is not on this list.[1][2][3][4]

Avoid in pregnancy:

  • All RAAS blockers: losartan, ramipril, amlodipine + olmesartan, and losartan + HCTZ. In the 2nd and 3rd trimesters they cause oligohydramnios, renal dysgenesis, skull hypoplasia, and fetal death. In ROPAC, first-trimester ACE-inhibitor use was also linked to congenital anomalies (OR 3.2).[5][6][7]
  • Atenolol: causes fetal growth restriction (SGA OR 2.3 vs metoprolol).[8]

Statins are no longer contraindicated in pregnancy since the FDA's 2021 change. They can be continued in familial hypercholesterolemia or established ASCVD, but they remain contraindicated during breastfeeding.[8][9]

The JACC review's central illustration below summarizes cardiovascular drug safety in pregnancy and lactation, colour-coded as safe, limited data, or contraindicated.[6]

Central Illustration Central Illustration. Cardiovascular Medications in Pregnancy Former Food and Drug Administration ABCDX categories: A) no demonstrated risk to the fetus based on well-controlled human studies; B) no demonstrated risk to the fetus based on animal studies; C) animal studies have demonstrated fetal adverse effects, no human studies, potential benefits may warrant use of the drug; D) demonstrated human fetal risk, potential benefits may warrant use of the drug; and X) demonstrated high risk for human fetal abnormalities outweighing potential benefit; N) nonclassified. ACE = angiotensin-converting enzyme; ARB = angiotensin receptor blocker; DOACs = direct oral anticoagulants; ERA = endothelin-receptor antagonists; INH = inhaled; IV = intravenous; PO = by mouth.

Where sources disagree

  • Amlodipine: a 2019 review lists it as not recommended in pregnancy. The ESC 2025, AHA/ACC 2025, and AHA 2022 consider it probably safe and comparable to nifedipine.[8][15][1][14]
  • Statins:
    • Older JACC reviews (2016, 2021) list them as contraindicated in pregnancy.
    • Since 2021 the FDA, ESC, and AHA allow use in high-risk pregnancy.
    • All sources agree statins are contraindicated during breastfeeding.[8][28][9][2]
  • Thiazides and indapamide in lactation:
    • The older HCTZ and indapamide labels advise choosing between the drug and breastfeeding.
    • The current HCTZ label, AFP, and the Circulation 2025 table consider standard doses safe, with possible milk suppression at higher doses.[29][17][10][12][18]
  • Clopidogrel in lactation: a 2016 JACC table says not recommended. The current label and LactMed report no harm in limited cases.[28][26][27]
  • Low-dose aspirin in lactation: the manufacturer advises against it. LactMed and the AHA consider low doses compatible.[6][4][25]
  • ACE inhibitors before conception: some sources advise stopping before conception. ROPAC found no need to stop long before pregnancy, as long as the drug is stopped once pregnancy is confirmed.[6][7]

Practical points

  • Switching off RAAS blockers or atenolol: move to nifedipine ER or labetalol (or metoprolol). AHA/ACC 2025 targets BP below 140/90 based on CHAP, where treatment cut the composite of severe preeclampsia, preterm birth, abruption, or fetal death by 18% (absolute) without increasing growth restriction.[1]
  • Postpartum and breastfeeding: first-line choices are nifedipine, amlodipine, enalapril, and labetalol. Metoprolol is the preferred β-blocker. ACE inhibitors can be restarted after delivery, using enalapril or captopril instead of ramipril.[5][10]
  • Nifedipine with magnesium sulfate: risk of hypotension and placental hypoperfusion when they are combined (as noted with the earlier endocrine and emergency list).[6]
  • Digoxin dosing: requirements rise in pregnancy and fall after delivery. Check levels and watch the neonate for toxicity (vomiting, arrhythmias).[3]
  • Rifampicin interaction (from the antibacterial list): it lowers nifedipine, amlodipine, metoprolol, atorvastatin, and digoxin levels (standard practice).

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Risk here depends on drug class and dose: valproate, topiramate, phenytoin, and carbamazepine carry known teratogenic signals, paroxetine has a cardiac signal, and lactation risk depends on infant sedation and milk transfer, particularly for long-acting benzodiazepines and doxepin.

Still open: lactation data for doxepin, clomipramine, duloxetine, flupentixol, the benzodiazepines, and the Z-drugs, plus pregnancy data for pregabalin, ethosuximide, pizotifen, and piracetam.

Still open: lactation data for the Z-drugs, midazolam, diazepam, and the SSRIs, and pregnancy data for pizotifen, piracetam, melitracen, and chlordiazepoxide.

Still open: valproate's neurodevelopmental data and lactation advice, clomipramine and nortriptyline milk transfer, and eszopiclone and chlordiazepoxide data.

Sertraline and escitalopram are the first-line antidepressants in pregnancy. Nortriptyline and imipramine are the preferred tricyclics during breastfeeding. Valproate is the highest-risk drug on this list and should be avoided in pregnancy whenever any alternative exists. Topiramate, phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and first-trimester paroxetine also carry established teratogenic risk. Doxepin should be avoided during breastfeeding. In epilepsy, antiseizure medications should not be stopped abruptly once pregnancy is confirmed, because uncontrolled seizures carry their own maternal and fetal risk. Ideally, switching to a lower-risk drug happens before conception.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

Most of these drugs are compatible with breastfeeding, especially when the mother took the same drug during pregnancy, since the fetus was already exposed to more drug than milk will deliver. Phenobarbital, ethosuximide, doxepin, and long-acting benzodiazepines are the main exceptions, because they reach high levels in the infant or cause infant sedation.[1][3][5][7]

Antiseizure medications and others

The Nordic cohort below (JAMA Neurology) shows neurodevelopmental outcomes by medication. Valproate and topiramate separate clearly from lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and carbamazepine. The 2026 ConcePTION case-control study found a ventricular septal defect signal with first-trimester gabapentinoid exposure (aOR >2), the only significant subgroup.[55][44]

Where sources disagree

  • Amitriptyline: the 2025 migraine guidelines in Cephalalgia advise avoiding it in pregnancy and lactation and stopping it 7 days before delivery. ACOG lists it as L2 for lactation, and the AHA notes that tricyclics have low teratogenic potential.[2][19][56]
  • Topiramate in lactation: the same migraine guideline advises against it. AES rates it as recommended, and LactMed reports most infants tolerate it.[40][43][56]
  • Clomipramine: the AHA says it passes into milk more than other tricyclics. LactMed considers it acceptable.[19][23]
  • Topiramate and autism: a Nordic cohort showed elevated neurodevelopmental risk, but a later population study did not replicate the autism signal after adjustment.[47][44]

Practical points

  • Epilepsy: never stop an antiseizure drug abruptly in pregnancy because of the risk of status epilepticus. Use the lowest effective dose; malformation risk rises with dose and with polytherapy. Folic acid before conception is standard; in one study, autistic traits were higher after valproate exposure when folate was not used.[4][40][41]
  • Valproate for migraine or bipolar disorder: contraindicated in pregnancy. Women of childbearing potential need highly effective contraception. Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, topiramate at higher doses) make hormonal contraception less effective.
  • Don't switch drugs just because of lactation: if a drug worked during pregnancy, continue it postpartum, since fetal exposure was greater than milk exposure will be.[1][9]
  • Late-pregnancy exposure: watch newborns for poor neonatal adaptation after SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, mirtazapine, or benzodiazepines.[27][18][25][10]
  • Sedating drugs while breastfeeding: another adult should be available to care for the infant, and bed-sharing should be avoided.[13]
  • Pregabalin plus opioids: observe the newborn for withdrawal.[49]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety here turns on gestational age for NSAIDs (FDA warnings at 20 and 30 weeks), CYP2D6 ultrarapid-metabolizer risk for tramadol in breastfed infants, and pethidine's accumulating metabolite. I'll check the guideline and lactation data for each agent.

Still open: morphine and pethidine lactation data, tolperisone, baclofen milk transfer, and lactation data for diclofenac, indomethacin, and the fenamates.

In pregnancy, paracetamol and lidocaine are the safe choices. In lactation, paracetamol, ibuprofen, lidocaine, colchicine, and low-dose short-course morphine are safe. Avoid every NSAID from 20 weeks on, and stop all of them, low-dose aspirin excepted, by 30 weeks. Avoid tramadol, pethidine, and the paracetamol + tramadol combination while breastfeeding. NSAIDs at or after about 20 weeks can cause fetal kidney injury and oligohydramnios. At or after about 30 weeks they can close the ductus arteriosus early.[1][2] The FDA advises against tramadol in breastfeeding: in CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers the infant gets too much active metabolite.[3][4] Pethidine's metabolite norpethidine builds up in infants and sedates them.[3]

Ibuprofen is the NSAID of choice in both pregnancy (second trimester only) and lactation, because it has the most data.[1][5]

NSAIDs

[1][3][6][5][11][4][16][2][14][7][8][12][17][13][9][10][15]

Paracetamol and opioids

[3][25][4][30][18][31][19][20][21][26][22][23][28][29][24][27]

Muscle relaxants, colchicine, and lidocaine

[32][40][36][33][41][7][37][38][39][34][35]

Where sources disagree

  • Paracetamol: in September 2025 the FDA alerted clinicians to a possible link with autism and ADHD and started a label change, while acknowledging that causation has not been established. ACMT, FIGO, ACOG, the WHO, and the EMA still consider it the safest analgesic in pregnancy. An umbrella review found no association in sibling-controlled analyses, and 2026 cohorts from Taiwan and Denmark found no link. Untreated maternal fever carries its own fetal risk.[42][18][20][19][43]
  • Naproxen in lactation: AFP discourages long-term use; the IHS cites newer evidence supporting it.[3][5]
  • NSAIDs in the first trimester: the ACOG-referenced position and the IHS restrict NSAIDs to the second trimester, given conflicting miscarriage data and a National Birth Defects Prevention Study signal for 10 anomalies. Other population studies show no increase.[6][5][11]
  • Tramadol malformations: the large Danish cohort was null, while Swedish and Ontario data show organ-specific signals.[26][23][27]

Practical points

  • Tocolysis: obstetric indomethacin for preterm labor is a specialist indication with its own gestational-age and duration limits. It is separate from analgesic use.
  • Late-pregnancy topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel) should also be avoided at or after 30 weeks.[6]
  • Postpartum multimodal analgesia is the standard: scheduled paracetamol + ibuprofen, with ketorolac after cesarean birth. Adding these regimens in place of IV morphine PCA reduced exclusive-breastfeeding failure.[4][22]
  • Opioids while breastfeeding: breastfeed before the dose, use the lowest dose for 2–3 days, and avoid other sedatives. Seek care urgently if the infant is unusually sleepy, feeds poorly, has trouble breathing, or is limp.[3][22]
  • Chronic opioid, baclofen, or tramadol use through delivery: observe the newborn for withdrawal.[32][25]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety for topicals turns on systemic absorption, so potency, body surface area, occlusion, and application near the breast matter more than the drug class. Topical retinoids, methoxsalen, and hydroquinone are the main concerns.

Still open: fusidic acid, topical tacrolimus and corticosteroids in lactation, and coal tar and benzoyl peroxide milk data.

Most topicals on this list are acceptable in pregnancy and breastfeeding when applied to limited areas. That includes azelaic acid, benzoyl peroxide, topical clindamycin, mupirocin, mild- to moderate-potency topical corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, calcipotriol at recommended doses, and emollients. In pregnancy, avoid all topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin, topical isotretinoin, and their combinations), hydroquinone, minoxidil, coal tar, and oral methoxsalen (PUVA). The retinoid advice is precautionary rather than based on harm. In a 2026 Nordic cohort, major malformations occurred in 3.3% of infants exposed to topical retinoids in the first trimester and 3.0% of unexposed infants (aRR 1.1). Accidental exposure therefore does not call for alarm.[1][2][3]

During breastfeeding, nearly all of these are compatible if kept off the nipple and areola. Use creams or gels rather than ointments on the breast, because infants who lick ointment can ingest mineral paraffin. The exceptions are oral methoxsalen (withhold breastfeeding for 24 hours after a dose), potent corticosteroids on the nipple, and coal tar.[4][5][6]

Acne agents

Topical corticosteroids and combinations

The low-birth-weight concern with potent steroids is shown in the Cochrane potency-stratified analysis below. Mild and moderate agents show no signal, while individual studies of potent and very potent agents do (UK cohort RR 2.08).[15]

Figure 2.3 Comparison 2 Stratified analysis by corticosteroid potency, Outcome 3 Low birth weight (cohort studies).

Other dermatologic agents

Where sources disagree

  • Topical retinoids: AAD prefers non-retinoids, and the EMA contraindicates them in pregnancy. The tretinoin label, a 2024 review that calls adapalene 0.1% safe, and the 2026 Nordic cohort all show no excess malformations.[11][12][10][1][2]
  • Potent corticosteroids and birth weight: the clobetasol label and older UK data show a dose-related low-birth-weight signal. A Danish cohort of 60,497 exposed pregnancies found no increase even with large cumulative amounts of potent steroids.[14][17][15]
  • Minoxidil in lactation: the AAP has classed it as compatible. The OTC label warns it may be harmful while breastfeeding, the Cochrane review says not to use it, and the oral tablet label says not to give it to nursing women.[36][32][37][34]
  • Topical tacrolimus in lactation: the label asks clinicians to choose between nursing and the drug. LactMed and guidelines consider it low risk and allow it on the nipple.[24][38]

Practical points

  • First-line acne regimen in pregnancy: azelaic acid, benzoyl peroxide, or clindamycin + benzoyl peroxide. Switch from any retinoid-containing product once pregnancy is confirmed.[1][39]
  • Steroid amount: track the grams dispensed. The AAD-NPF threshold is under 60 g/week, and the label signal is above 300 g of potent steroid across the pregnancy. Step down to hydrocortisone or clobetasone where possible.[4][14]
  • Breast and nipple: apply right after a feed and gently clean before the next one. Use creams or gels, not ointments. Never use potent steroids, retinoids, or hydroquinone on the areola.[24][6]
  • Postpartum hair loss: this is usually telogen effluvium, which resolves on its own. That makes it easy to avoid minoxidil during breastfeeding.

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety for this group depends on sedation and anticholinergic load in the infant with first-generation antihistamines, on how much pregnancy data each second-generation agent has, and on the neuropsychiatric boxed warning for montelukast.

Still open: lactation data for each antihistamine and montelukast, the Danish fexofenadine cohort results, and data for ketotifen, rupatadine, pheniramine, and butamirate.

Cetirizine (with loratadine) is the preferred antihistamine in both pregnancy and breastfeeding. Fexofenadine is a well-supported alternative. Intranasal or inhaled fluticasone and montelukast are acceptable in both. Use first-generation antihistamines only as occasional single doses. Avoid hydroxyzine in early pregnancy and long-term near delivery. Rupatadine, oral ketotifen, and butamirate have too little data and should be replaced with better-studied drugs.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

During breastfeeding, the second-generation agents give the infant very little drug (cetirizine relative infant dose about 2%). First-generation agents can sedate the infant and cause poor feeding. Any antihistamine can reduce milk supply, especially at higher doses, when combined with pseudoephedrine, or before lactation is well established.[7][8][9][10]

H1-antihistamines

Montelukast, fluticasone, and butamirate

Topical fluticasone cream was covered with the dermatologic agents. Low-to-moderate potency use is acceptable, and the same nipple precautions apply.[26]

Where sources disagree

  • Hydroxyzine: the label contraindicates it in early pregnancy and while nursing, citing inadequate human data and fetal abnormalities in rodents at high doses. AFP lists it as acceptable in pregnancy, and LactMed accepts occasional small doses.[16][2][17]
  • Antihistamines in lactation: most manufacturers' labels advise avoiding them, mainly because data are lacking. The BSACI, LactMed, and a systematic review consider cetirizine and loratadine compatible, with RID under 5% for every antihistamine studied.[27][9][28]
  • Montelukast neuropsychiatric risk: in 2020 the FDA added a boxed warning (agitation, depression, sleep disturbance, suicidality) and reserved montelukast for rhinitis that has not responded to alternatives. Observational studies, including a large FDA cohort, have been mixed or null.[29][30][31]

Practical points

  • Allergic rhinitis: an intranasal corticosteroid is first-line in both pregnancy and lactation. Add cetirizine or loratadine if needed. Avoid oral decongestants in the first trimester, and avoid pseudoephedrine before milk supply is established.[2][23]
  • Asthma: do not stop inhaled corticosteroids or montelukast that are controlling asthma. Poorly controlled asthma raises the risk of preeclampsia, prematurity, and low birth weight.[22][4]
  • Montelukast postpartum: given the boxed warning, watch for mood or behavior changes during the period of postpartum depression risk. Stop the drug if new neuropsychiatric symptoms appear.[29]
  • First-generation agents near delivery: avoid regular use late in the third trimester because of neonatal sedation and, with hydroxyzine, withdrawal. While breastfeeding, give them as a single dose after the last evening feed.[19][18]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety in this group turns on how much first-trimester data each agent has, particularly ondansetron's orofacial cleft signal, and on domperidone's cardiac risk when used to boost milk supply. Pregnancy and lactation data for the PPIs, antiemetics, and the less-studied antispasmodics need checking.

Still open: lactulose in breastfeeding, and any drug-specific pregnancy or lactation data for mebeverine, alverine, and tiemonium.

Safe in both pregnancy and breastfeeding: aluminium/magnesium hydroxide antacids, famotidine, lactulose, and omeprazole or pantoprazole. Ondansetron and prochlorperazine are acceptable second-line antiemetics. Ondansetron has a small oral-cleft signal with first-trimester use: adjusted RR 1.24, about 3 extra cases per 10,000 treated women, with no increase in cardiac malformations. For that reason, guidelines either individualize its use before 10 weeks or, in the EMA's case, advise against it in the first trimester.[1][2][3]

Avoid or replace three groups:

  • Antispasmodics (tiemonium, alverine, mebeverine) in pregnancy, because their safety hasn't been established.[4]
  • Racecadotril in pregnancy, because there are no human data.
  • Domperidone used to boost milk supply. The FDA warns against it because of QT prolongation and sudden cardiac death. It is not approved for lactation in any country.[5]

Several drugs on this list differ from the earlier lists in being better than "acceptable" during breastfeeding. Ondansetron (RID 3.7%), pantoprazole (0.14%), famotidine, lactulose, and antacids reach infants in negligible amounts.[6][7][8][9]

Acid suppressants and antacids

Antiemetics and prokinetics

The US Medicaid cohort below shows the ondansetron signal. Associations with cardiac and overall malformations disappear with full confounder adjustment, while the oral-cleft signal persists at every level of adjustment.[1]

Figure 1 Risk of Congenital Malformations in Infants Following Exposure to Ondansetron During the First Trimester: Main Analyses

Antidiarrhoeal, laxative, and antispasmodics

Where sources disagree

  • Ondansetron in the first trimester: ACOG and RCOG support it as second-line. Systematic reviews in a 2026 Lancet review found no significant increase in major malformations, cardiac defects, or clefts. The absolute cleft risk would rise from about 0.11% to 0.14% if the association is causal. In 2019 the EMA advised against first-trimester use, and the European SmPC also advises against breastfeeding. That conflicts with the US label's lactation data.[15][3][6]
  • Domperidone to increase milk supply: the FDA cites QT prolongation, torsades, and sudden death, and calls the efficacy evidence limited. Meta-analyses found about 90 mL/day more milk in mothers of preterm infants, with no excess maternal side effects. Arrhythmias have occurred only in women with prior arrhythmia history. LactMed notes that doses above 30 mg/day may increase arrhythmia risk.[5][20][26][21]
  • PPIs: ACG rates every PPI as low risk in both pregnancy and lactation. One meta-analysis found a malformation OR of 1.28, and AFP limits PPIs to the second and third trimesters. A Lancet review advises avoiding esomeprazole and rabeprazole while breastfeeding.[8][12][10]

Practical points

  • Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy: start with doxylamine–pyridoxine or another H1-antihistamine. Escalate to a phenothiazine, metoclopramide, or domperidone, and then to ondansetron. Reserve corticosteroids for refractory hyperemesis.[15][27][8]
  • Reflux in pregnancy: lifestyle measures first, then an antacid, alginate, or sucralfate, then famotidine, then omeprazole or pantoprazole.[14]
  • Antacids and supplements: take antacids at least 2 hours apart from iron and folic acid.[7]
  • Racecadotril with an ACE inhibitor (e.g., ramipril from the cardiovascular list): angioedema risk rises because both block bradykinin breakdown.[28]
  • Domperidone for nausea (where marketed): standard practice is up to 10 mg three times daily for no more than 7 days, avoiding QT-prolonging drugs and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Stop it immediately if palpitations, dizziness, or syncope occur.[21]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety here hinges on glucose-lowering choice in pregnancy (insulin preferred, with metformin and sulfonylureas crossing the placenta), levothyroxine dose escalation, and agent-specific concerns such as dopamine suppressing prolactin and prolonged magnesium sulfate affecting fetal bone.

Still open: gliclazide-specific data, adrenaline for anaphylaxis in pregnancy, folic acid dosing, folinic acid and mecobalamin, and intrapartum dextrose and crystalloid effects on the neonate.

Safe in both pregnancy and breastfeeding: levothyroxine, iron–folic acid combinations, folic acid, mecobalamin, IV crystalloids, and adrenaline for anaphylaxis. The only point to watch is giving them correctly.

The diabetes drugs are where caution is needed:

  • Insulin is preferred in pregnancy. Metformin and the sulfonylureas cross the placenta.
  • Sulfonylureas: stop them at least 2 weeks before delivery, because they can cause prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia.
  • Linagliptin: avoid in pregnancy because there are too few data.
  • Magnesium sulfate: keep continuous use to 5–7 days or less. Longer exposure causes fetal hypocalcemia and bone demineralization.[1][2][3][4]

During breastfeeding, nearly everything here is compatible:

  • Metformin: under 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose reaches the infant.
  • Tranexamic acid: milk levels are about 1% of serum levels.
  • Magnesium: levels rise only slightly in milk, and infants absorb it poorly.
  • Sulfonylureas and linagliptin: prefer alternatives with newborn or preterm infants, and watch the infant for hypoglycemia.
  • Dopamine infusion: lowers prolactin.[5][6][7][8][9][10]

Antidiabetic and thyroid agents

Haematinics, folates, and haemostatics

Emergency, critical care, and IV fluids

Where sources disagree

  • Metformin:
    • ADA and the Endocrine Society/ESE prefer insulin. They cite placental transfer, offspring adiposity signals, and a doubling of small-for-gestational-age infants in one trial in type 2 diabetes. For type 2 diabetes, they do not consider metformin a substitute for insulin.
    • It remains an option in GDM when insulin is not feasible, and not all professional bodies agree on restricting it.[1][11][2]
  • Sulfonylureas in pregnancy: guidelines advise switching to insulin. The gliclazide cohort and decades of glimepiride experience show no malformation signal, but neonatal hypoglycemia remains a concern.[3][13]
  • High-dose folic acid: US sources recommend 4 mg/day and European guidance 5 mg/day for high-risk patients.[24][26][25]
  • Magnesium in lactation: older labels advise caution because magnesium appears in milk. The current label and LactMed consider infant effects unlikely.[7][45][4]
  • Tranexamic acid:
    • The oral tablet label says it is not indicated in pregnancy, and the injection label notes there are no first-trimester data.
    • Obstetric trials support its use for postpartum hemorrhage.[6][31][32]

Practical points

  • Levothyroxine timing: take it on an empty stomach, at least 4 hours apart from iron, calcium, and antacids (standard practice). Recheck TSH every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy.[17]
  • Iron absorption: iron combinations absorb poorly with PPIs and antacids from the GI list. Separate iron from antacids by at least 2 hours. Alternate-day oral dosing may reduce GI side effects.[46][47]
  • Sulfonylurea before delivery: if a sulfonylurea was used, stop it at least 2 weeks before delivery and monitor neonatal glucose.[3]
  • Magnesium with nifedipine: use caution with nifedipine (from the cardiovascular list). Together they can cause additive hypotension and neuromuscular blockade. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output, and keep calcium gluconate available (standard practice).
  • Postpartum glucose control: metformin and insulin are the preferred choices while breastfeeding. Glipizide or glyburide are better-studied sulfonylureas than gliclazide or glimepiride if one is needed.[5][8]

Original OpenEvidence explanations and notes

Source text below retains all original caveats, bibliographies, conflicts, figures, practical remarks, and follow-up questions. No clinical safety statement has been independently audited.

Safety in this group turns on the corticosteroid choice (prednisolone is largely inactivated by the placenta, while dexamethasone crosses to the fetus), on cyclophosphamide's first-trimester teratogenicity, on the dose limits for vitamin A, and on iodine exposure from povidone-iodine.

Still open: corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide in breastfeeding, tadalafil and dapoxetine, calcium and vitamin C/E supplementation trials, and amlexanox.

Still open: dapoxetine, amlexanox, tadalafil in breastfeeding, dexamethasone in breastfeeding, and upper limits for vitamin D and zinc in pregnancy and lactation.

Safe in both pregnancy and breastfeeding: prednisolone and methylprednisolone, the ocular lubricants, riboflavin, B-complex, vitamin C, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate, zinc, and beta-carotene, all at standard doses. Prednisolone and methylprednisolone are preferred for maternal disease because the placenta inactivates them and less than 10% reaches the fetus.[1][2]

Avoid or restrict these:

  • Cyclophosphamide: absolutely contraindicated in the first trimester. Use it in the 2nd or 3rd trimester only for life-threatening disease, and avoid it while breastfeeding.[3][4]
  • Baricitinib: avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.[5]
  • Dexamethasone: use only for fetal indications.[1]
  • Vitamin A (retinol): keep below 10,000 IU/day, because higher doses are teratogenic in the first 60 days after conception.[6]
  • Povidone-iodine mouthwash: use for 14 days or less, or switch to chlorhexidine. Iodine can cause transient hypothyroidism in the fetus or breastfed infant.[7][8]

Dapoxetine and tadalafil are not indicated in women. Tadalafil does have a role in pulmonary arterial hypertension in pregnancy.[9][10]

Systemic corticosteroids, JAK inhibitor, and cyclophosphamide

Where sources disagree

  • High-dose steroids and the timing of breastfeeding:
    • The ACR recommends delaying breastfeeding or discarding milk for 4 h after doses of prednisone 20 mg/day or more.
    • LactMed and the 2026 global IBD consensus consider this delay unnecessary.
    • For IV methylprednisolone pulses, a 2026 lupus review suggests waiting 2–4 h.[12][13][15][4]
  • Cyclophosphamide and breastfeeding:
    • The label advises no breastfeeding until 1 week after the last dose.
    • Pharmacokinetic modeling suggests 1–3 days of discarding milk gets the relative infant dose below 1%, but active metabolites were not measured.[39][40][21]
  • Vitamin A: the WHO accepts up to 10,000 IU/day where deficiency is common. NICE advises avoiding supplements in developed settings, which means intake above about 700 µg/day.[6]
  • Separating calcium from iron:
    • The WHO advises taking calcium a few hours apart from iron–folic acid.
    • A 2022 programmatic review says separation is unnecessary.[33][34]
  • Zinc upper limit: 25 mg/day (EFSA) versus 40 mg/day (IOM).[35]

Practical points

  • Steroids and diabetes control: prednisolone and dexamethasone raise glucose. In women on metformin or insulin from the endocrine list, or with gestational diabetes, check glucose more often during courses (standard practice).[2]
  • Calcium carbonate and levothyroxine: take them at least 4 h apart (standard practice). Calcium carbonate also doubles as the preferred antacid in pregnancy.[41]
  • Before cyclophosphamide or baricitinib: confirm a negative pregnancy test and effective contraception. The cyclophosphamide label requires pregnancy testing before starting.[18][21]
  • Tadalafil with nitrates: never combine with nitroglycerin from the cardiovascular list. Use caution with prazosin because of additive hypotension (standard practice).
  • Dapoxetine and serotonergic drugs: do not combine with SSRIs, SNRIs, or TCAs from the CNS list (serotonin syndrome risk; standard practice).
